taxonomy.subtopic: ATP7B dysfunction, impaired biliary copper excretion, and low ceruloplasmin

questions.stem_html:
A 19-year-old college student develops tremor, personality change, and jaundice. Slit-lamp examination reveals brown rings at the corneal periphery. Serum ceruloplasmin is low, and 24-hour urinary copper excretion is elevated. Liver biopsy shows increased copper.

Which transport defect causes this disorder?

options.text_html: Failure of intestinal ferroportin to export iron into portal blood
Reduced renal reabsorption of cystine and dibasic amino acids
Failure of a hepatocellular P-type ATPase to excrete copper into bile and incorporate it into ceruloplasmin
Absent synthesis of alpha-1 antitrypsin in hepatocytes

questions.explanation_html: ATP7B moves copper into bile and enables incorporation into apoceruloplasmin. Loss of function leads to hepatic copper retention, low circulating ceruloplasmin, and copper deposition in brain and cornea. The phenotype and laboratory pattern are explained by ATP7B failure at the hepatocyte's biliary copper-export pathway.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Ferroportin defects alter iron handling, not copper accumulation with Kayser-Fleischer rings.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: This causes Gaucher disease, which features lipid-laden macrophages rather than copper overload.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: This is cystinuria and produces recurrent stones, not hepatic and neurologic copper toxicity.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency involves protein misfolding and elastase injury, not ATP7B-mediated copper transport.

questions.educational_objective: Identify Wilson disease and connect ATP7B dysfunction to impaired biliary copper excretion, low ceruloplasmin, urinary copper elevation, hepatic injury, and neurologic disease.
